issues.legal_issue: Substituted service is insufficient to support an ex parte decree when the serving officer does not follow the required procedure after failing to find the defendant and the court authorizes substituted service without recording the required satisfaction.
material_facts: Summons sent to the defendant’s stated address were returned unserved after the bailiff was told that the defendant had left the premises and was residing elsewhere.
The bailiff’s report did not state that a copy of the summons had been affixed to a conspicuous part of the house.

The trial court mechanically allowed substituted service without recording satisfaction that the defendant was avoiding service or that service in the ordinary way could not be effected for another reason.
The plaintiff relied on publication in a newspaper, and the defendant did not appear; the suit proceeded ex parte and was decreed.
The defendant challenged the ex parte decree in a first appeal, and the High Court set it aside.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in setting aside the ex parte judgment and decree because the prescribed service procedure had not been followed and the order authorizing substituted service did not show the required application of mind. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order V Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when a serving officer cannot find the defendant after due and reasonable diligence and the specified conditions are met, the officer must affix a copy of the summons to a conspicuous part of the relevant house and report the circumstances. Order V Rule 20 makes substituted service an exception to ordinary service and requires the court to be satisfied that the defendant is keeping out of the way to avoid service or that service in the ordinary way cannot be effected for another reason; the court’s order must show due consideration of those requirements. The Civil Manual, Chapter III, paragraphs 33–36, emphasizes following the prescribed service procedures and assessing whether service is proper. Newspaper publication did not cure the antecedent failure to comply with the required procedure.

rule.if: first_appeal_from_ex_parte_decree and defendant_not_found_at_service_address and summons_not_affixed_at_house and substituted_service_order_lacks_required_satisfaction

predicates.first_appeal_from_ex_parte_decree: The defendant challenged an ex parte decree in a first appeal.
predicates.defendant_not_found_at_service_address: The serving officer could not find the defendant at the address where service was attempted.
predicates.summons_not_affixed_at_house: The serving officer did not affix a copy of the summons to a conspicuous part of the relevant house after failing to find the defendant.
predicates.substituted_service_order_lacks_required: The court authorized substituted service without recording the required basis for finding that ordinary service could not be effected or was being avoided.

issues.definition: When a defendant challenges an ex parte decree in a first appeal, the decree is set aside if the defendant was not found at the service address, the summons was not affixed at the house, and the court’s substituted-service order lacked the required satisfaction.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant may challenge an ex parte decree by first appeal, including on the grounds that the material in the ex parte proceedings did not entitle the plaintiff to a decree or that the suit should not have proceeded ex parte.
material_facts: The defendant challenged the ex parte decree by filing a first appeal.
The High Court found adequate grounds to set aside the decree, including defects in the service process and in the order authorizing substituted service.
issues.conclusion: A first appeal was an available remedy, and the defendant established adequate grounds in that appeal to set aside the ex parte decree.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 96(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, as explained in Bhanu Kumar Jain v Archana Kumar and followed in Rabindra Singh v Financial Commissioner, Cooperation, Punjab and Mahesh Yadav v Rajeshwar Singh, an appeal against an ex parte decree may be based on the contention that the material brought on record in the ex parte proceedings does not entitle the plaintiff to a decree, or that the suit should not have been posted for ex parte hearing. A defendant may pursue an appeal and an application to set aside the decree for non-appearance simultaneously; filing the latter does not remove the right of appeal. The judgment also states that, after dismissal of an appeal arising from the application to set aside the decree, the same contention cannot be raised in a first appeal.

predicates.defendant_challenges_ex_parte_decree_by_: The defendant challenges a decree made in the defendant’s absence by filing a first appeal.
predicates.ex_parte_material_does_not_entitle_plain: The material placed before the court in the defendant’s absence does not entitle the plaintiff to the decree granted.
predicates.suit_should_not_have_proceeded_ex_parte: The suit should not have been heard in the defendant’s absence.

issues.definition: A first appeal may set aside an ex parte decree when the defendant challenges it and either the material presented in the defendant’s absence does not support the decree or the suit should not have proceeded in the defendant’s absence.
